planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and hold seedlings near 50-55F for 10-14 days once several true leaves have formed to encourage reliable first-year bud set; transplant after frost danger has passed into deeply worked, fertile soil.

directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into deep, richly amended soil in full sun once frost danger has passed. Emerald is a spineless, dark green annual hybrid bred as a seed-grown alternative to older perennial artichoke types, forming a slightly more compact plant than some annual comparisons while still setting a good number of medium, tightly furled buds in its first season. It shares the same need for a brief cool spell after transplanting to trigger uniform first-year flowering, and it holds up well to the heat of long, dry summers once established. Keep the soil evenly moist and fertile through the growing season and harvest buds while the scales are still closed tight for the best texture.
sources: Harris Seeds -- Emerald artichoke variety description
University of California Cooperative Extension -- Artichoke Production Guide

planting.note: Transplant rooted divisions or seedlings after last frost into deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Romanesco is the traditional round-headed heirloom type long grown around Rome and typically needs a full season or overwintered crown before it flowers heavily.

directions: Transplant into deep, fertile, well-drained soil worked with compost, siting plants in full sun with room to form a large clump. Romanesco is a classic Italian heirloom type from the countryside around Rome, producing broad, rounded, purple-flushed green buds with fleshy, nearly spineless scales and a tender heart, the type traditionally used for carciofi alla romana. As a true perennial type it is slower to reach full production than seed-grown annual hybrids, generally needing an established second-year crown for its heaviest harvest, though in mild coastal climates it can be grown as a long-season annual from an early transplant. Cut buds while the scales are still tightly closed and before they begin to spread open for the best flavor and texture.
sources: Slow Food Foundation -- Ark of Taste
University of California Cooperative Extension -- Artichoke Production Guide

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and give seedlings 10-14 days near 50F once several true leaves have formed to promote earlier, more uniform bud set; in mild zone 9 winters, a late-summer sowing for fall transplant is also common in commercial production.

directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into deep, rich, well-drained soil in full sun once frost danger has passed. Talpiot is an Israeli-bred F1 hybrid developed alongside Tavor for seed-propagated, first-year annual production, forming a large, vigorous, spineless plant that sets medium green buds over a long harvest window. It shares the strong heat tolerance of other Israeli annual artichoke selections, making it a dependable choice for hot-summer growing regions, and continues to push side buds after the central bud is harvested. Keep soil consistently moist and fertile through the season and cut buds while the scales are still tight, before they begin to loosen and spread.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension -- Artichoke Production Guide
American Society for Horticultural Science -- artichoke cultivar trial literature

planting.note: Start indoors six to eight weeks before last frost and transplant after frost danger has passed into deep, fertile soil; Cardy was bred to self-blanch as it grows, so it needs little or no wrapping or earthing-up before harvest.

directions: Sow indoors and transplant into deep, well-drained soil enriched with compost, in full sun with steady moisture through the growing season. Cardy is a modern cardoon selection bred to naturally pale and mellow its leaf ribs as the plant matures, largely eliminating the traditional multi-week job of bundling and wrapping stalks in cardboard or straw to exclude light. The tall, silvery, deeply cut foliage still makes an imposing ornamental clump even where it is not harvested, and a light earthing-up of the base in the final weeks before cutting can further improve rib color and tenderness. Harvest the thick leaf stalks in autumn once they have filled out, trimming away the spiny leaf blades before cooking.
